What Factors Are Most Strongly Associated with Wins?

Author

Khushi Chaturvedi

Published

April 10, 2026

1. Introduction

This report analyzes the NHL 2022–2023 regular season dataset (32 teams) to identify which variables are most strongly associated with W (Wins) regulation wins using Exploratory Data Analysis and linear regression.

2. Exploratory Data Analysis

Code 
library(tidyverse)
library(corrplot)
library(broom)
library(car)
library(knitr)

# Load data
df <- read.csv("nhl_2223.csv")

# Dataset dimensions
cat("Rows:", nrow(df), "| Columns:", ncol(df))
Rows: 32 | Columns: 18

3. Correlation Analysis

Code 
# Select numeric columns (exclude GP — zero variance, all teams = 82)
num_df <- df %>% select(W, PTS, Reg_PTS, ROW, PPG, DIFF, RW, GF, SOW, SOG, SOL, OTL, GA, L)

# Correlation with W, sorted
corr_w <- cor(num_df) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  select(W) %>%
  filter(rownames(.) != "W") %>%
  arrange(desc(W))

kable(round(corr_w, 4), caption = "Pearson Correlation with W (Wins)")
Pearson Correlation with W (Wins)
W
PTS 0.9878
Reg_PTS 0.9819
ROW 0.9813
PPG 0.9776
DIFF 0.9692
RW 0.9632
GF 0.7965
SOW 0.2270
SOG 0.2054
SOL 0.0526
OTL -0.3588
GA -0.8873
L -0.9481
Code 
corr_df <- corr_w %>%
  rownames_to_column("Variable") %>%
  rename(Correlation = W) %>%
  arrange(Correlation)

corr_df$Variable <- factor(corr_df$Variable, levels = corr_df$Variable)

ggplot(corr_df, aes(x = Correlation, y = Variable, fill = Correlation > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Correlation, 3),
                hjust = ifelse(Correlation >= 0, -0.1, 1.1)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#e74c3c", "#2980b9")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.5) +
  xlim(-1.2, 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Correlation of Each Variable with W (Wins)",
       x = "Pearson Correlation", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
Code 
top_vars <- df %>% select(W, PTS, Reg_PTS, ROW, DIFF, GF, GA, L, PPG)
cor_matrix <- cor(top_vars)

corrplot(cor_matrix,
         method = "color",
         type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black",
         number.cex = 0.7,
         tl.cex = 0.85,
         col = colorRampPalette(c("#e74c3c","white","#2980b9"))(200),
         title = "Correlation Heatmap — Key Variables",
         mar = c(0,0,1,0))
Code 
top4 <- c("DIFF","GF","GA","L")

plots <- map(top4, function(var) {
  r_val <- round(cor(df[[var]], df$W), 3)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[var]], y = W)) +
    geom_point(color = "#2980b9", size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = Team), size = 2.5, vjust = -0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(title = paste0("W vs ", var, "  (r = ", r_val, ")"),
         x = var, y = "Wins (W)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
})

library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(grobs = plots, ncol = 2)

Note: Variables like PTS, ROW, and Reg_PTS have near-perfect correlations with W because they are mathematically derived from W. They are excluded from regression to avoid circularity. DIFF = GF − GA, so including all three would create perfect multicollinearity.

# Fit model using GF and GA (excludes DIFF to avoid perfect multicollinearity)
model <- lm(W ~ GF + GA, data = df)
model_summary <- summary(model)

5. Model Assumptions

Code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Residuals vs Fitted
plot(model, which = 1,
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted",
     col = "#2980b9", pch = 19)

# Q-Q Plot
plot(model, which = 2,
     main = "Q-Q Plot of Residuals",
     col = "#2980b9", pch = 19)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

5.1 Linearity

The scatter plots (Figure 3) and the Residuals vs. Fitted plot (Figure 5, left) show no systematic curvature the linearity assumption is satisfied.

5.2 Normality

The Q-Q plot (Figure 5, right) shows residuals closely following the normal line. The normality assumption is reasonably satisfied.

5.3 Multicollinearity (VIF)

Code 
vif_vals <- vif(model)
kable(data.frame(Variable = names(vif_vals),
                 VIF = round(vif_vals, 3),
                 Assessment = ifelse(vif_vals < 5, "✅ OK (< 5)", "⚠️ High")),
      caption = "Variance Inflation Factors")
Variance Inflation Factors
Variable VIF Assessment
GF GF 1.376 ✅ OK (< 5)
GA GA 1.376 ✅ OK (< 5)

Both VIF values are ≈ 1.38, well below the threshold of 5. No multicollinearity issue.

5.4 Homoscedasticity

The Residuals vs. Fitted plot shows no fan or funnel shape the homoscedasticity assumption holds.

6. Conclusions

Code 
insights <- data.frame(
  Rank = 1:3,
  Variable = c("DIFF (Goal Difference)", "GA (Goals Against)", "GF (Goals For)"),
  `r with W` = c(0.969, -0.887, 0.797),
  Interpretation = c(
    "Best single summary of team dominance",
    "Defensive quality is strongly tied to wins",
    "Offense matters, but slightly less than defense"
  )
)
kable(insights, caption = "Top Predictors of W (Wins)")
Top Predictors of W (Wins)
Rank Variable r.with.W Interpretation
1 DIFF (Goal Difference) 0.969 Best single summary of team dominance
2 GA (Goals Against) -0.887 Defensive quality is strongly tied to wins
3 GF (Goals For) 0.797 Offense matters, but slightly less than defense
  • The model W ~ GF + GA achieves R² = 0.94, explaining 94% of the variance in regulation wins.
  • Both GF (+0.153 per goal) and GA (−0.164 per goal) are highly significant (p < 0.001).
  • The GA coefficient is slightly larger in magnitude, suggesting defensive performance is marginally more impactful than offense.
  • Shootout statistics (SOW, SOL, Pct_SO) show near-zero correlation with W shootout results are essentially random noise.
  • Future analyses should include multi-season data or game-level data for more robust inference.

# 1. Introduction

This report analyzes the NHL 2022–2023 regular season dataset (32 teams) to identify which variables are most strongly associated with **W (Wins)** regulation wins using Exploratory Data Analysis and linear regression.

# 2. Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(corrplot)
library(broom)
library(car)
library(knitr)

# Load data
df <- read.csv("nhl_2223.csv")

# Dataset dimensions
cat("Rows:", nrow(df), "| Columns:", ncol(df))
```

```{r}
#| label: summary
kable(summary(df[, c("W","GF","GA","DIFF","L","PTS","ROW")]), 
      caption = "Descriptive Statistics — Key Variables")
```

# 3. Correlation Analysis

```{r}
#| label: correlation-table

# Select numeric columns (exclude GP — zero variance, all teams = 82)
num_df <- df %>% select(W, PTS, Reg_PTS, ROW, PPG, DIFF, RW, GF, SOW, SOG, SOL, OTL, GA, L)

# Correlation with W, sorted
corr_w <- cor(num_df) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  select(W) %>%
  filter(rownames(.) != "W") %>%
  arrange(desc(W))

kable(round(corr_w, 4), caption = "Pearson Correlation with W (Wins)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-corr-bar
#| fig-cap: "Figure 1: Correlation of each variable with W (Wins)"

corr_df <- corr_w %>%
  rownames_to_column("Variable") %>%
  rename(Correlation = W) %>%
  arrange(Correlation)

corr_df$Variable <- factor(corr_df$Variable, levels = corr_df$Variable)

ggplot(corr_df, aes(x = Correlation, y = Variable, fill = Correlation > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Correlation, 3),
                hjust = ifelse(Correlation >= 0, -0.1, 1.1)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#e74c3c", "#2980b9")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.5) +
  xlim(-1.2, 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Correlation of Each Variable with W (Wins)",
       x = "Pearson Correlation", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Figure 2: Correlation Heatmap — Key Variables"

top_vars <- df %>% select(W, PTS, Reg_PTS, ROW, DIFF, GF, GA, L, PPG)
cor_matrix <- cor(top_vars)

corrplot(cor_matrix,
         method = "color",
         type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black",
         number.cex = 0.7,
         tl.cex = 0.85,
         col = colorRampPalette(c("#e74c3c","white","#2980b9"))(200),
         title = "Correlation Heatmap — Key Variables",
         mar = c(0,0,1,0))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatters
#| fig-cap: "Figure 3: Wins vs. Top Predictor Variables"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

top4 <- c("DIFF","GF","GA","L")

plots <- map(top4, function(var) {
  r_val <- round(cor(df[[var]], df$W), 3)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[var]], y = W)) +
    geom_point(color = "#2980b9", size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = Team), size = 2.5, vjust = -0.7, alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(title = paste0("W vs ", var, "  (r = ", r_val, ")"),
         x = var, y = "Wins (W)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
})

library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(grobs = plots, ncol = 2)
```

> **Note:** Variables like PTS, ROW, and Reg_PTS have near-perfect correlations with W because they are *mathematically derived* from W. They are excluded from regression to avoid circularity. DIFF = GF − GA, so including all three would create perfect multicollinearity.

# 4. Linear Regression Model

```{r}
#| label: model

# Fit model using GF and GA (excludes DIFF to avoid perfect multicollinearity)
model <- lm(W ~ GF + GA, data = df)
model_summary <- summary(model)
model_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: model-table

kable(tidy(model) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 4))),
      caption = "Regression Coefficients — W ~ GF + GA")
```

```{r}
#| label: model-metrics

cat("R-squared:     ", round(model_summary$r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Adjusted R²:   ", round(model_summary$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("F-statistic:   ", round(model_summary$fstatistic[1], 2), "\n")
cat("p-value:       ", pf(model_summary$fstatistic[1],
                          model_summary$fstatistic[2],
                          model_summary$fstatistic[3],
                          lower.tail = FALSE))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-actual-pred
#| fig-cap: "Figure 4: Actual vs. Predicted Wins"

df$predicted <- predict(model)

ggplot(df, aes(x = W, y = predicted)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2980b9", size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#e74c3c",
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Team), size = 2.8, vjust = -0.7, alpha = 0.75) +
  labs(title = "Actual vs. Predicted Wins",
       x = "Actual Wins", y = "Predicted Wins") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

# 5. Model Assumptions

```{r}
#| label: fig-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Figure 5: Residual Diagnostics"
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Residuals vs Fitted
plot(model, which = 1,
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted",
     col = "#2980b9", pch = 19)

# Q-Q Plot
plot(model, which = 2,
     main = "Q-Q Plot of Residuals",
     col = "#2980b9", pch = 19)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 5.1 Linearity
The scatter plots (Figure 3) and the Residuals vs. Fitted plot (Figure 5, left) show no systematic curvature the linearity assumption is **satisfied**.

## 5.2 Normality
The Q-Q plot (Figure 5, right) shows residuals closely following the normal line. The normality assumption is **reasonably satisfied**.

## 5.3 Multicollinearity (VIF)

```{r}
#| label: vif

vif_vals <- vif(model)
kable(data.frame(Variable = names(vif_vals),
                 VIF = round(vif_vals, 3),
                 Assessment = ifelse(vif_vals < 5, "✅ OK (< 5)", "⚠️ High")),
      caption = "Variance Inflation Factors")
```

Both VIF values are ≈ 1.38, well below the threshold of 5. **No multicollinearity issue.**

## 5.4 Homoscedasticity
The Residuals vs. Fitted plot shows no fan or funnel shape the **homoscedasticity assumption holds**.

# 6. Conclusions

```{r}
#| label: conclusions-table

insights <- data.frame(
  Rank = 1:3,
  Variable = c("DIFF (Goal Difference)", "GA (Goals Against)", "GF (Goals For)"),
  `r with W` = c(0.969, -0.887, 0.797),
  Interpretation = c(
    "Best single summary of team dominance",
    "Defensive quality is strongly tied to wins",
    "Offense matters, but slightly less than defense"
  )
)
kable(insights, caption = "Top Predictors of W (Wins)")
```

- The model **W ~ GF + GA** achieves **R² = 0.94**, explaining 94% of the variance in regulation wins.
- Both **GF** (+0.153 per goal) and **GA** (−0.164 per goal) are highly significant (p < 0.001).
- The **GA coefficient is slightly larger in magnitude**, suggesting defensive performance is marginally more impactful than offense.
- **Shootout statistics** (SOW, SOL, Pct_SO) show near-zero correlation with W shootout results are essentially random noise.
- Future analyses should include multi-season data or game-level data for more robust inference.
